title: Alone in the forest (325–333)
hookLine: if you find no good companion, walk alone like an elephant in the forest

cards: A table for one. A weekend with no plans. A quiet apartment on a Saturday night.
For some people, being alone can feel like proof that something's wrong, so it's tempting to fill the silence with company, even company that leaves you worse off.
Today's verses have a different picture: a great elephant walking by itself through the forest, unhurried, needing nothing from the herd.
The commentary says the Buddha himself once spent a rainy season like that, in a forest, with an elephant for a companion.

teach.b: The elephant chapter ends with verses about the mind and about company.
First the mind: it used to wander wherever it pleased, one verse says, but now I will hold it, the way a trainer with a hook holds an elephant in rut.
Pull yourself out of the bad road like an elephant pulling itself out of the mud. Then company.
If you find a wise, good friend to walk with, walk with them gladly. If you don't, walk alone.

Verse three hundred thirty, in Max Müller's English: "It is better to live alone, there is no companionship with a fool; let a man walk alone, let him commit no sin, with few wishes, like an elephant in the forest."
The commentary sets these verses after a bitter quarrel among the monks of Kosambi, yesterday's city.
The monks wouldn't make peace, so the Buddha left and spent a rains retreat in the Parileyya forest, where, the story says, a great elephant who had also left his noisy herd looked after him.
Notice what the verse doesn't say. It doesn't say people are bad or that friendship is a trap. Earlier chapters praised good company, and the next verse says friends are sweet when need comes.
Good company first; if that's missing, your own company, kept clean and simple, beats bad company.
This week you cut the forest, traded for the bigger joy, stayed well awake, grasped it rightly, guarded the border town and bore the arrow. The elephant closes the week walking by itself, content.

how: Buddhist tradition values both good spiritual friendship and time in solitude; monks go on solitary retreats, and the Parileyya elephant who served the Buddha appears in Buddhist temple art.

o: a hermit who has given up on friendship for good
one who walks alone when no good companion is found
a wanderer with no home who begs from town to town

games.q: match each piece of today's verses and story.
p: where an elephant served the Buddha

s: the verses say friendship is a trap
they say walk with a good friend gladly; alone only when good company is missing.
the commentary says the Buddha spent a rains retreat with an elephant
in the Parileyya forest, after the monks of Kosambi quarreled.
verse 330 praises living alone with many wishes
it says walk alone, with few wishes, like an elephant in the forest.

games.q: the only company on offer this weekend is a group that always leaves you drained and a little meaner. what do today's verses suggest?
o: go anyway; any company beats none.
walk alone this time, and keep looking for good friends.
give up on friends for good.
games.why: the verses put a good friend first; if there's none, your own company, kept simple, beats bad company.

practice: For this sit, you are the elephant in the forest: no one needs anything from you, and you need nothing from anyone.
Listen to whatever sounds are near, the way an elephant listens to the trees, and notice how it feels, a little strange, maybe, or a relief.
If loneliness shows up, let it sit beside you like another animal in the clearing; you don't have to send it away.

wordCard.voice: Ekacara. One who walks alone: with no good companion, walk alone, with few wishes, like an elephant in the forest.

orig.note: Pali ekacara: one who walks alone; verse 330 uses the verb 'eko care' (let one walk alone).

carryVoice: Your line: alone, not lonely. Your own company can be good company. Day two hundred seventeen, and a week, done.

sources.work: The Dhammapada (Sacred Books of the East, vol. 10)
